walkmanStory.title: A tape recorder that gave up recording.
walkmanStory.text: Sony's engineers started from a portable cassette recorder made for journalists. They removed the recording circuit and the speaker, added stereo playback and light headphones, and kept a second jack so two people could listen. It went on sale in Japan on 1 July 1979.

walkmanStory.title: Music became something you carried.
walkmanStory.text: Abroad it first sold as the Soundabout (USA), the Stowaway (UK) and the Freestyle (Sweden). The Walkman name won and became the everyday word for any personal stereo. The second jack and the Hotline button were made for sharing; later models dropped them as listening turned private.

walkmanStory.title: Replaced, then replaced again.
walkmanStory.text: The Discman D-50 put the compact disc in a pocket in 1984. MP3 players such as the Rio PMP300 removed the medium altogether in 1998. In 2010 Sony stopped producing cassette Walkmans in Japan.

walkmanStory.title: Worth keeping, worth writing down.
walkmanStory.text: Rubber belts soften, heads gather oxide, batteries leak. A cared-for TPS-L2 still plays. Its passport records what was replaced, by whom, and why the object matters.

specifications: Compact Cassette, stereo playback only (no recording, no speaker)
Two 3.5 mm headphone jacks, marked A and B
Play, stop/eject, fast forward, rewind; orange Hotline button with built-in microphone
Two AA batteries or an external adapter
originalUses: Music left the living room: in the street, on the bus, on a run.
Jack A and jack B let two people listen to the same cassette.
The Hotline button lowered the volume and opened a microphone.
preservation: Take them out: old batteries leak and corrode the contacts.
Expect to replace them: rubber drive belts soften and turn sticky with age.
Clean the tape path: head, capstan and pinch roller with isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab.
Cool, dry, away from magnets: heat warps plastic and magnets damage tapes.
modelTimeline: Cassette Walkman production ends in Japan

notes: Both channels clean; slight hiss on jack B
Light scuffs on the aluminium side

repairLog: Drive belt replaced; speed checked against a test tape
At a repair café, by a volunteer
objectTimeline: Found in a drawer, contacts cleaned
Belt replaced at a repair café
sample.memory: Bought second-hand in 1987. It played the same two tapes all summer, and the second jack meant my brother never had to ask.

labOutcomes.name: Repair
labOutcomes.involves: Diagnose the fault, find the part, and record the repair in the object's passport. Repair cafés and makerspaces can help.

labOutcomes.name: Reuse
labOutcomes.involves: Give it a daily job again: a dedicated music player, a games machine, a phone for emergencies.

labOutcomes.name: Donate
labOutcomes.involves: Offer it to a school, club, museum or collector who will use or keep it. Pass its passport on with it.

labOutcomes.name: Preserve
labOutcomes.involves: Clean it, store it safely, document it fully, and keep it as a record of how people lived with technology.

labOutcomes.name: Recover parts
labOutcomes.involves: Remove working components (screens, drives, buttons, boards) and list them for people repairing the same model.

labOutcomes.name: Recycle
labOutcomes.involves: Take it to a certified e-waste collection point so metals and plastics are recovered and hazardous parts handled safely.

mission: An object can lose its commercial value without losing its historical, practical, cultural or emotional value. RELIK documents those values before the object disappears, and helps people decide what should happen next.
